name: Adam Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a marketing specialist at Northfell Outdoor. We make walking boots, tents and rain jackets. I run the campaigns for the boots range, write product pages, plan the emails, and work with the hiking clubs we sponsor. I use AI tools all day: first drafts, sorting customer reviews, testing headlines.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the testing. I can try six versions of a boot page on Monday and know by Friday which sells. I also like the weekend trips with the hiking clubs, getting photos in the mud. What wears me down is meetings that could have been one line in a chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I'd still use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are worth it if you put the work in, and the people who wrote them off were too quick. Online I'd post a few before and after results from the boot pages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'm in a strong spot. I'm the one at Northfell who gets the most out of these tools. Freya and I have a good cushion, and my brother Nils and I own a small flat we rent out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and ask for a raise at my review in January, with the test results to back it up. I'd also put more into the rental flat, a new kitchen, so we can raise the rent fairly next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which routine tasks would the tools take off you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sorting the reviews and writing the size guides. I already hand those to the AI. It frees me up for the hiking club work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything on your mind outside of AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Freya works nights at the hospital, and it's hard on her. Getting married and starting a family is more on my mind than any computer. Probably in a couple of years.

I'd post **before and after** results from the boot pages.
think: I'm in a **strong spot**, getting the most from the tools.
We have a good cushion plus a **rental flat** with my brother Nils.
do: Ask for a **raise** in January with test results.
Fit a **new kitchen** in the rental flat.
Raise the **rent fairly** next year once the kitchen is done.

fieldNote: He's **secure** and already ahead on the tools.
His real focus is **marriage and family**.

steps.text: Ask Northfell for a raise in January using test results
Fit a new kitchen in the rental flat he owns with Nils

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's pretty much what I see coming, yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, not a threat, for people who work hard and pick things up. I'd say it at work and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I come out of it well. Northfell needs fewer writers, but it needs someone who runs the tools and can show the numbers. That's me. I do feel for older colleagues like Ruth, who's been writing the catalogue for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to set up the AI system for the whole marketing team, so I'm the one who runs it. I'd ask for a team lead role. And I'd start a small business on the side, selling hiking maps and guides I make with AI, to test whether I can make money on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Sorry for Ruth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ruth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to teach her. My colleague Ruth knows the customers better than anyone, and the AI tools can't fake that. If Ruth learns the tools, she's worth more, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think government should help people like Ruth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, maybe, for training. But I'd rather the company did it, and people stepped up. Handouts don't teach anybody anything.

I'd say it **at work** and mean it.
think: I **come out well**, because Northfell needs someone to run the tools.
I feel for **older colleagues** like Ruth.
do: Set up the **AI system** for the whole marketing team.
Start a side business selling **hiking maps** made with AI.
S1.quote: My colleague Ruth knows the customers better than anyone, and the AI tools can't fake that. If Ruth learns the tools, she's worth more, not less.
fieldNote: His **self-reliance** shapes both his plan and his views on help.
He'd **teach** a colleague rather than step over her.
Starting a **side business** shows his risk appetite.

steps.text: Set up an AI writing system for Northfell's marketing team
Sell hiking maps and guides made with AI online

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's quick even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to get moving now, not wait for someone to save them. I wouldn't wait for someone to save me. I'd post about the side projects I'd be starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, being good with the tools stops being a job by itself. If AI does any thinking work, Northfell doesn't need me to run it. The only thing left is owning something, a business or property, not selling my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the side business while there's a gap, and I'd use our savings to buy a second rental flat with Nils. I'd stay at Northfell as long as they'd pay me, but I'd expect to go within a year of it arriving. Freya's nursing is hands-on, so she'd have about three years more than me, which matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared, but my stomach knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still plan the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. We'd marry next year, small, family and church, no big party. Children might wait a couple of years, though, and I don't love that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd put savings into property while your income could go. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. Rent is paid by people living somewhere, and people will still need somewhere to live. I'd rather own the roof than be a writer with cash in the bank.

fieldNote: Even he expects to **lose his job** within a year of arrival.
He bets on **property**, a free-market instinct.

steps.text: Spend evenings and weekends growing the hiking maps business
Buy a second rental flat with his brother Nils
Hold a small church wedding next year and delay children

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty to build something if you start now. I'd tell younger people at Northfell to start a side project this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is my sweet spot. I'd be 32. I can grow a business on the side and get Northfell to pay me while I do. When it arrives, I want to be the owner, not the staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the hiking maps business to the point where it pays a salary, maybe in three years. Then I'd leave Northfell. I'd buy one more rental flat with Nils and use AI for the bookings and repairs. Freya could drop to part-time nights if she wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. Like before a big hike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the maps business once AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it might get copied in a day. That's why the flats matter. The hiking maps business is the fast money, and the rental flats are the slow money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when the robots come for hands-on work three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then nursing changes too, and Freya's job might go. That's when I'd want the flats paying the bills. It's a ten-year plan squeezed into eight.

fieldNote: He splits his plan into **fast and slow** money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best time in a century to start something, and I'd say it everywhere, at work, online and at the hiking clubs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is great for me. I'd be 37 when it arrives. I can raise a family, build a business and own a few flats by then, if I don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Northfell two years, get the team lead role, and learn how the business side works. Then I'd start my own outdoor brand, small, maybe just socks and gaiters, run with AI from day one. Freya and I would marry next year and try for children soon after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Properly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk you're not seeing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that everyone has the same idea, starting small brands with AI. Then it's a crowded shop. I'd need the hiking clubs on my side, the real people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say get a trade and stay put. My mum would say marry Freya first. Mum would win.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to build anything before it arrives. What would help is fewer rules on starting a small business, and lower taxes for people who hire, so people can create work instead of waiting for it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about families. People talk about jobs as if everyone's alone. My partner Freya and I plan everything together, and that's what gets you through.

headlineQuote: People talk about jobs as if everyone's alone. My partner Freya and I plan everything together, and that's what gets you through.
portrait: Adam, 27, runs **boot campaigns** at Northfell Outdoor and uses AI tools all day.
He has a strong cushion and owns a **rental flat** with his brother Nils.
He stays calm in Steady Disruption, expecting to **run the tools** and start a side business.
In AGI by 2028 he's anxious and bets on **owning property**, not selling his time.
With more time he plans his **own brand**, marriage to Freya and children.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: **Fewer rules** for small businesses and **lower taxes** for people who hire.
